ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *meh₂-der. Proto-Germanic *maiz Proto-Germanic *maistaz Proto-Germanic *maist Proto-West Germanic *maist Old English mǣst Middle English most English most From Middle English most, moste, from Old English mǣst, māst, from Proto-Germanic *maistaz, *maist. Cognate with Scots mast, maist (“most”), Saterland Frisian maast (“most”), West Frisian meast (“most”), Dutch meest (“most”), German meist (“most”), Danish and Swedish mest (“most”), Icelandic mestur (“most”).

senses.d: Forms the superlative of many adjectives.
ex: This is the most important example.
Correctness is most important.

senses.d: With a superlative adjective ending in -est.
ex: the most tallest building in the world

senses.d: To a great extent or degree; highly; very.
ex: This is a most unusual specimen.
Most cruel edict! Sure, thy generous soul, Septimius, abhors the dreadful task of persecution.

senses.d: The greatest; the best.
The greater part of a group, especially a group of people.
ex: Most want the best for their children.
The peach was juicier and more flavourful than most.

senses.d: The greatest amount.
ex: The most I can offer for the house is $150,000.

senses.d: The greater part.
ex: Most of the penguins were friendly and curious.
Most of the rice was spoiled.

senses.d: A record-setting amount.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French trés, from Old French trés, inherited from Latin trāns, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of trans-, trans, and tré-.
From extrême + -ment.

pt:muito.gl: very; a lot; very much (to a great extent or degree)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese muito, from Latin multus (“much; many”), from the Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Aragonese muito, Catalan molt, Galician moito, Italian molto, Romanian mult, Spanish mucho.
From extrema + -mente.

ety.text: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito (“gnat”), diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca (“fly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūs- (“fly, stinging fly, gnat”). Cognate with West Flemish meuzie (“mosquito”), dialectal Swedish mausa (“fly”), Lithuanian musė (“a fly”) and Sicilian muschitta (“midge”). See also midge. First attested in the 1580s.

senses.d: A small flying insect of the family Culicidae, the females of which bite humans and animals and suck blood, leaving an itching bump on the skin, and sometimes carrying diseases like malaria, dengue and yellow fever.
ex: We lit a driftwood fire to help keep the mosquitoes away. It was partially successful.

senses.d: To fly close to the ground, seemingly without a course.

grp.label: small flying insect of the family Culicidae, known for biting and sucking blood

ety.text: Borrowed from Spanish mosquito, diminutive of mosca, from Latin musca, whence also the French doublet mouche (“a fly”). The metathesis of /k/ and /t/ might have been due to influence of tique (“a tick”).
From Paraguayan Guarani mbarigui.
From Late Latin zinzala, of imitative origin.
Inherited from Old Spanish mosquito, from mosca + -ito. Cognate with Sicilian muschitta (“midge”), Italian moschetto. Doublet of mosquete (“musket”)
Latin plāgalbor. Spanish plaga Learned borrowing from Latin plāga. Doublet of llaga.

Borrowed from Spanish mosquito, from Old Spanish mosquito, from mosca + -ito. By surface analysis, mosca + -ito. Piecewise doublet of mosquete.

pt:melga.gl: some species of mosquitoes, usually found in swamp areas

senses.d: A place of worship for Muslims, often having at least one minaret; a masjid.
ex: There's a mosque near where I live.

senses.d: Any of various small, green, seedless plants growing on the ground or on the surfaces of trees, stones, etc.; now specifically, a plant of the phylum Bryophyta (formerly division Musci).
ex: Another says you should tense your body, look up in the air, and think about cool moss.

senses.d: A kind or species of such plants.

ex: Spanish moss
Irish moss

senses.d: A bog; a fen.
ex: the mosses of the Scottish border

senses.d: To become covered with moss.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French mosse (“moss”), from Frankish *mosa (“moss”), from Proto-Germanic *musą (“moss”). For the culinary sense one might suspect influence by Dutch moes, German Mus (both “mush, purée”).

From Latin mūscus, probably through a diminutive Vulgar Latin root *mūsclus, from syncopation of an earlier *mūsculus. Compare Romanian mușchi, Friulian muscli. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mus-.
Inherited from Old Spanish musgo, from Latin muscus; probably a semi-learned term.

ety.text: From most + -ly. The sense “probably” is a calque from Indian languages such as Tamil அனேகமாக (aṉēkamāka).

senses.d: Mainly or chiefly; for the most part; usually, generally, on the whole.
ex: They're mostly good people, although they have made a few mistakes.

senses.d: To the greatest extent; most.
ex: She was to be their chosen visitor, she was to be for weeks under the same roof with the person whose society she mostly prized [...]!

senses.d: Synonym of probably, likely.
